utf-8.name: UTF-8
utf-8.definition: A variable-length Unicode encoding using one to four bytes per scalar value.
utf-8.explanation: UTF-8 preserves ASCII byte values and represents other Unicode scalar values with multi-byte sequences. Rust strings guarantee valid UTF-8, but a byte vector may contain incomplete or invalid sequences. Token boundaries in byte BPE can split a multi-byte character, so decoding each token independently as text is unsafe. Concatenate token bytes first and validate the complete result when a text boundary requires it. Byte counts, token counts, and Unicode scalar-value counts therefore answer different questions and should always be labeled.

byte-pair-encoding.name: byte-pair encoding
byte-pair-encoding.definition: A tokenizer fitted by repeatedly replacing frequent adjacent symbol pairs with new symbols.
byte-pair-encoding.explanation: Byte BPE starts with 256 symbols, one for every byte, and estimates an ordered list of merge rules from adjacent counts. Each new token represents the concatenation of two earlier tokens. Encoding begins from bytes and applies rules by learned rank; decoding concatenates stored byte strings. The byte base guarantees coverage and exact round trips. The maximum merge count, actual rule count, merge order, boundary policy, tie-breaking, pre-tokenization, and normalization are part of tokenizer identity because changing them can change token IDs consumed by a model.

round-trip.name: round trip
round-trip.definition: The invariant that decoding an encoded byte sequence reproduces the original bytes exactly.
round-trip.explanation: A round-trip test compares bytes rather than displayed strings: decoding an encoding must recover exactly the original bytes. It catches overlapping replacements, incorrect learned-token bytes, invalid IDs, and serialization-order mistakes. Multilingual examples are valuable because UTF-8 characters span different byte lengths and token boundaries may split them. Exact round trip establishes reversibility, not compression quality or model accuracy. A reloaded tokenizer should satisfy the same invariant and produce identical token IDs when deterministic compatibility matters.
